are built together as AND–OR circuits, sharing AND gates where possible:
. What is the minimum number of AND gates?
An exhaustive search over all sets of shared product terms finds no cover with 3 AND gates.

nx-dl-03-04-q08.concept: In multi-output design a non-prime term ($AB'C$) can be worth it if several outputs use it.

c: That builds each output's own minimal SOP without sharing.
is implemented as a two-level NAND–NAND circuit (complements available, gates of any fan-in). How many gate inputs does the circuit have in total?
First level: one 2-input NAND per term:
Second level: one 3-input NAND combining them: 3 inputs.

nx-dl-03-04-q09.concept: Gate inputs = literals in the first level + terms entering the output gate.

c: The output gate's three inputs count too.
That is the number of gates, not of gate inputs.
Which of the following statements about static hazards in two-level circuits are true?
A function whose 1-cells are pairwise non-adjacent (such as parity) can still have a static-1 hazard in its minimal SOP.
Adding the consensus of two of its terms to an SOP never changes the function it computes.
A minimal SOP is always free of static-1 hazards.
A two-level OR–AND (POS) circuit can have a static-0 hazard.
(A) False: a static-1 hazard needs two adjacent 1-cells (a single change from one 1 to another); with no adjacent 1s every single change leaves the 1-set.
(D) True: dually, adjacent 0-cells in different sum terms give a momentary 1.

nx-dl-03-04-q10.concept: Hazards come from adjacent 1-cells (or 0-cells) in different terms; the consensus term fixes them without changing the function.

c: Minimisation removes consensus terms, which is exactly what creates hazards.
POS circuits have the dual problem: static-0 hazards.

absorption.title: Absorption and the loss of associativity
absorption.intro: A toy format with 4 fraction bits: x = 32 = 1.0000 × 2⁵ and y = 1 = 1.0000 × 2⁰. The next float above 32 is 34 (ulp = 2).

elements.text: Absorption: a small number added to a large one (4 fraction bits)
ulp(32) = 2 here, so half an ulp is 1

steps.caption: Align y to x's exponent 5: shift its significand right 5 places. The 1 lands just past the 4 kept bits: 0.0000 with guard bit 1 and round bit 0.
The extra bits are exactly half an ulp (G = 1, R = S = 0): a tie. Ties go to the even neighbour, and 1.0000 is even, so x + y rounds to 32. y has been absorbed.
Add 1 again: the same thing happens, so (32 + 1) + 1 = 32.
Now add the small numbers first: 1 + 1 = 2 exactly. Aligning 2 = 1.0000 × 2¹ to exponent 5 shifts it 4 places: 0.0001, with nothing left over. 32 + 2 = 1.0001 × 2⁵ = 34 exactly.
So (32 + 1) + 1 ≠ 32 + (1 + 1): floating-point addition is not associative. Adding the small terms first keeps them from being absorbed.

set.text: order matters: add small numbers first

arithmetic-shift.title: Arithmetic and logical shifts
arithmetic-shift.intro: The 8-bit pattern of −7, 11111001. Shifted copies will appear underneath.

steps.caption: Arithmetic shift right: every bit moves one place right, the last bit falls off, and the sign bit is copied into the empty top place. 11111001 → 11111100 = −4.
−7 ÷ 2 = −3.5, and the shift gave −4: an arithmetic right shift divides by 2 and rounds down (towards −∞), not towards zero.
A logical shift right fills the top with 0 instead. 01111100 = 124: fine for unsigned numbers, wrong for negative ones.
Shift left (arithmetic and logical are the same): a 0 enters at the right. 11110010 = −14 = 2 × (−7). It is exact because the top two bits of x were equal, so no significant bit was lost.

assoc-test.title: The associativity test for NAND
assoc-test.intro: To test whether an operator is associative, compare (a ⋆ b) ⋆ c with a ⋆ (b ⋆ c) on every row.

elements.text: Is NAND associative? Compare both bracketings on all 8 rows

steps.caption: Fill the column (a↑b)↑c: first NAND a with b, then NAND the result with c. Algebraically it is ab + c′.
Fill the column a↑(b↑c): it is a′ + bc.
The columns disagree on rows 001, 011, 100, 110. One disagreeing row is enough: NAND is not associative.
The same 8-row test works for any operator defined by a table: compute both bracketings and compare. AND, OR, XOR and XNOR pass it; NAND, NOR and implication fail.

base-carry-column.title: Column addition in base 8
base-carry-column.intro: Two octal numbers lined up by place: 37 above 45. Carries will appear above the columns.

elements.text: Adding (37)₈ + (45)₈: a column that reaches 8 carries

steps.caption: Units column: 7 + 5 = 12. In base 8, twelve is one eight and four units, so write 4 and carry 1 into the eights column.
Eights column: 3 + 4 + the carry 1 = 8. That is exactly one 64 and no eights, so write 0 and carry 1 again.
Nothing is left to add except the carry, so it becomes the leading digit: (37)₈ + (45)₈ = (104)₈.
Check in decimal: 31 + 37 = 68, and (104)₈ = 64 + 4 = 68.

bcd-plus-six.title: BCD addition and the +6 correction
bcd-plus-six.intro: 386 and 457 in BCD, one 4-bit group per decimal digit. We add digit by digit from the right.

steps.caption: Units: 6 + 7 = 13 > 9, so add 0110: 1101 + 110 = 1 0011. Digit 3, decimal carry 1.
Tens: 8 + 5 + carry 1 = 14 > 9, so add 0110: 1110 + 110 = 1 0100. Digit 4, decimal carry 1.
Hundreds: 3 + 4 + carry 1 = 8, not above 9: no correction.
The result 1000 0100 0011 is BCD 843 = 386 + 457. Each +6 skipped the six unused patterns 1010 … 1111, so the carry came out at ten.

bcd-vs-binary.title: BCD versus binary
bcd-vs-binary.intro: Top: 59 in BCD, two 4-bit groups 0101 (5) and 1001 (9), each with weights 8 4 2 1. Bottom: 59 in pure binary, 111011, six bits with weights 32 to 1. BCD spends 8 bits where binary needs 6, and reading the BCD pattern as plain binary gives 89.

elements.text: 59 in BCD and in pure binary
read as binary, the BCD pattern 0101 1001 would be 89, not 59

bias-order.title: Biased exponents keep the unsigned order
bias-order.intro: Eight 3-bit exponent fields with their unsigned value, their 2's-complement value, and their value in excess-4 and excess-3.

elements.text: A 3-bit exponent field read in three codes
Unsigned order runs top to bottom.

steps.caption: The fields 000 … 111 are listed in unsigned order, top to bottom. A comparator that reads them as unsigned numbers puts each row above the one before it.
Read as 2's complement, the order breaks between 011 (+3) and 100 (−4): the bigger field holds the smaller exponent. A float with exponent −1 (111) would compare above one with exponent +3 (011).
Excess-4 (bias 2³⁻¹ = 4) subtracts 4 from the unsigned value: −4, −3, …, +3. The exponents now rise exactly as the fields rise.
Excess-3 (bias 2³⁻¹ − 1, the IEEE choice) gives −3 … +4, also in order. IEEE then reserves the end fields 000 and 111 for zero, denormals, infinity and NaN.

bitpair-table.title: Bit-pair recoding table
bitpair-table.intro: The eight multiplier triples and the radix-4 partial product each one selects.

steps.caption: Each radix-4 digit pairs two Booth digits: D = 2d(i+1) + d(i) = −2q(i+1) + q(i) + q(i−1). The eight triples give the digits 0, ±1, ±2.
So −29 = 0·4³ − 2·4² + 1·4 − 1: four radix-4 digits, at most four partial products for 8 bits, each a shift of ±M or ±2M.

block-sets.title: Unknown blocks in a circuit of functions, by minterm sets
block-sets.intro: Four-variable functions as rows 0–15. The circuit computes f = f₁·f₂ + f₃ with f₁ = Σ(1, 3, 5, 7, 9), f₂ = Σ(3, 7, 9, 12) and the target f = Σ(3, 7, 9, 14).

elements.text: Solving f = f₁·f₂ + f₃ for the unknown block

steps.caption: AND is intersection: f₁·f₂ = Σ(3, 7, 9). These rows are already supplied by the AND gate.
The target is f = Σ(3, 7, 9, 14). First check that f₁·f₂ lies inside f; it does, so a solution exists.
OR is union, so f₃ must supply every row of f that the AND does not: f₃ must contain row 14.
f₃ must also stay inside f (any extra row would appear in the output). So f₃ = Σ(14) plus any subset of {3, 7, 9}: f − f₁f₂ ⊆ f₃ ⊆ f.

booth-scan.title: Booth recoding: a sliding pair window
booth-scan.intro: The 8-bit multiplier −29 = 11100011 with a 0 appended on the right (q₋₁). A window covers the current bit and the bit to its right.

elements.text: Booth recoding of −29 = 11100011: slide a 2-bit window

steps.caption: i = 0: the window holds (q0, q₋₁) = (1, 0), so d0 = 0 − 1 = −1 (a run of 1s starts here: subtract M).
i = 1: the window holds (q1, q0) = (1, 1), so d1 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
i = 2: the window holds (q2, q1) = (0, 1), so d2 = 1 − 0 = +1 (a run of 1s ended just below: add M).
i = 3: the window holds (q3, q2) = (0, 0), so d3 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
i = 4: the window holds (q4, q3) = (0, 0), so d4 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
i = 5: the window holds (q5, q4) = (1, 0), so d5 = 0 − 1 = −1 (a run of 1s starts here: subtract M).
i = 6: the window holds (q6, q5) = (1, 1), so d6 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
i = 7: the window holds (q7, q6) = (1, 1), so d7 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
Read the digits MSB first: 0 0 −1 0 0 +1 0 −1 = −32 + 4 − 1 = −29. Three operations instead of five additions (one per 1): the run of three 1s at the top costs a single subtraction.

bubble-push.title: Bubble pushing turns NAND into a bubbled OR and NOR into a bubbled AND
bubble-push.intro: A NAND gate, drawn the usual way: an AND body with a bubble (inversion) on its output.

elements.text: Bubble pushing: De Morgan in pictures
NAND = AND with an output bubble

steps.caption: A NAND gate is an AND gate followed by NOT. Its output is 0 only when both inputs are 1: the column (AB)′ reads 1, 1, 1, 0.
Push the bubble backwards through the gate. Two things change: the body flips from AND to OR, and the one bubble splits into a bubble on every input.

set.text: the same gate drawn as an OR with bubbled inputs

steps.caption: Check it: A′ + B′ is 1 unless both A and B are 1, exactly the NAND column. This is De Morgan's law (AB)′ = A′ + B′.
The same move turns a NOR into an AND with bubbled inputs: (A + B)′ = A′B′. Both are 1 only on row 00.

set.text: NOR drawn as an AND with bubbled inputs

steps.caption: The rule: moving bubbles across a gate swaps AND and OR and complements every input and output it crosses. Two bubbles on one wire cancel.

circuit-read.title: Reading a three-gate circuit, one level at a time
circuit-read.intro: Three gates: G1 is a NAND of A and B, G2 an OR of B and C, and G3 an AND of the two results.

elements.text: Reading a circuit: label every gate, then follow the signals

steps.caption: Set the inputs A = 0, B = 1, C = 0. B feeds two gates (a fan-out), so it appears twice.
Level 2. F = AND(G1, G2) = 1·1 = 1. Every gate waited for its inputs: values flow left to right, one level at a time.
Set the inputs A = 1, B = 1, C = 0. B feeds two gates (a fan-out), so it appears twice.
Level 2. F = AND(G1, G2) = 0·1 = 0. Only G1 changed, and that was enough to change F.
Written as an expression, the circuit is F = (AB)′(B + C): G1 and G2 are the two factors, G3 multiplies them.

code-tables.title: Decimal digits in four codes
code-tables.intro: A table of the digits 0 to 9 in 8421 BCD, excess-3, 2421 and 4-bit Gray code. For example 5 is 0101 in BCD, 1000 in excess-3, 1011 in 2421 and 0111 in Gray; 9 is 1001, 1100, 1111 and 1101.

column-add-carry.title: Binary column addition with a moving carry
column-add-carry.intro: Two bytes, 181 and 110, written one above the other. The small row on top will hold the carries.

elements.text: Adding 10110101 + 01101110, one column at a time

steps.caption: Column 0: 1 + 0 = 1, which is 1 in binary: write 1, no carry.
Column 1: 0 + 1 = 1, which is 1 in binary: write 1, no carry.
Column 2: 1 + 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 3: 0 + 1 + carry 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 4: 1 + 0 + carry 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 5: 1 + 1 + carry 1 = 3, which is 11 in binary: write 1, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 6: 0 + 1 + carry 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 7: 1 + 0 + carry 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
The carry out of column 7 becomes a ninth bit: the sum is 1 0010 0011 = 291 = 181 + 110. In an 8-bit register the 1 would be the carry flag.

complement-subtraction.title: Complement subtraction with the end-around carry
complement-subtraction.intro: M = 1010100 (84). We will subtract N = 1000011 (67) using only an adder and bit inversion.

elements.text: 84 − 67 with the 1's complement and the end-around carry

steps.caption: Write N = 1000011 (67) and flip every bit: N̄ = 0111100. This is the 1's complement, 2⁷ − 1 − 67 = 60.
Add M + N̄ = 1010100 + 0111100 = 1 0010000. The sum is 144 = 2⁷ + 16: a carry comes out of the top bit because M > N.
End-around carry: remove the carry (worth 2⁷) and add it back as 1 at the bottom. Removing 2⁷ leaves M − N − 1 = 16; adding 1 corrects the 'one short' of the 1's complement.
Result 0010001 = 17 = 84 − 67. Had there been no carry, the result would have been negative, with magnitude equal to the 1's complement of the sum.

complement-tree.title: Complementing an expression: swap operators, complement literals
complement-tree.intro: The expression f = (A + B′C)(A′ + D) drawn as a tree: operators inside, literals at the leaves.

elements.text: Complement = swap every operator, complement every literal

steps.caption: General De Morgan, rule 1: swap every operator, AND ↔ OR. The root AND becomes an OR, the two ORs become ANDs, and the inner AND becomes an OR.
Rule 2: complement every literal. A becomes A′, B′ becomes B, C becomes C′, A′ becomes A and D becomes D′.
Read the new tree back, keeping its grouping: the root is now an OR, so f′ = A′(B + C′) + AD′. A truth table over all 16 rows confirms it is 1 exactly where f is 0.

completeness-checklist.title: Functional completeness by Post's five classes
completeness-checklist.intro: Each row is a set of gates; each column one of Post's five closed classes.

elements.text: Post's test: a set must escape all five classes
T0: 0-preserving · T1: 1-preserving · S: self-dual · M: monotone · A: affine. ✓ = some member is outside the class.

steps.caption: NAND escapes every class: NAND(0, 0) = 1, NAND(1, 1) = 0, it is not self-dual, not monotone (0 → 1 lowers it) and not affine. Complete on its own.
AND and OR are both monotone (and 0- and 1-preserving): they can never produce a complement. Not complete.
XOR and NOT are both affine (x ⊕ y and x ⊕ 1): every circuit of them is an XOR of inputs and constants. Not complete.
AND escapes the self-dual and affine classes, NOT escapes the preserving and monotone ones: together they escape all five. Complete.
Implication escapes everything except 1-preservation (1 → 1 = 1). Not complete alone; add the constant 0 and it is.
Majority is self-dual, monotone, 0- and 1-preserving. Not complete, even with free constants (constants are monotone).
The 2:1 MUX preserves 0 and 1, so alone it is not complete; with the constants 0 and 1 it is (it then makes NOT and AND).

consensus-cells.title: The consensus theorem on the rows of a truth table
consensus-cells.intro: Three product terms over x, y, z, each drawn as the set of rows where it is 1.

elements.text: Consensus: yz is already covered by xy and x′z

steps.caption: Each cell is one row xyz of the truth table. The term xy is 1 on rows 110 and 111.
The term x′z is 1 on rows 001 and 011.
The consensus term yz is 1 on rows 011 and 111. Row 111 is already in xy (there x = 1) and row 011 is already in x′z (there x = 0).
So adding yz adds no new 1: xy + x′z + yz = xy + x′z. Whatever x is, one of the first two terms already covers yz.

set.text: yz lies inside xy + x′z, so it is redundant

cyclic-map.title: The cyclic function Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) and its two minimal covers
cyclic-map.intro: Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) on a 3-variable map (rows A, columns B C).

elements.text: A cyclic function: no essential prime implicant

steps.caption: Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6): every 1 except the corners of the cube 000 and 111. Each 1 has exactly two neighbouring 1s, so it can be looped in two different pairs.
The six pairs form a ring: 1–3, 3–2, 2–6, 6–4, 4–5, 5–1. All six are prime implicants and every 1 is in two of them, so no prime implicant is essential.
Pick every other pair around the ring: B′C + A′B + AC′. Three pairs, 6 literals, every 1 covered once.
Or start one step further round: A′C + BC′ + AB′. Also three pairs and 6 literals. Two different minimal SOPs: the minimal form is not unique.

dont-care-toggle.title: Using don't-cares only where they enlarge a loop
dont-care-toggle.intro: Σm(1, 3, 7, 11, 15) + d(0, 5) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D); X marks a don't-care.

elements.text: Don't-cares: use an X only if it makes a loop bigger
Use an X only if it helps

steps.caption: f = Σm(1, 3, 7, 11, 15) + d(0, 5). The X cells may be treated as 1 or as 0, whichever gives the cheaper expression; they never need to be covered.
Column C D = 11 (m3, m7, m15, m11) is a quad of 1s: CD.
m1 is left. Without don't-cares its best loop is the pair m1, m3: A′B′D, 3 literals.
Treat X at m5 as 1: m1, m3, m5, m7 become a quad, A′D, with only 2 literals. The X at m0 would not enlarge any loop, so it stays 0 and is left out.

doubling-peel.title: Repeated doubling: 0.625 to binary
doubling-peel.intro: We will double the fraction again and again. Each integer part that pops out is one bit after the point.

elements.text: 0.625 to binary: double, peel off the integer part

steps.caption: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.25 for the next round.
0.25 × 2 = 0.5. The integer part 0 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.5 for the next round.
0.5 × 2 = 1. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0 for the next round. The fraction left is 0, so the expansion stops: 0.625 has a finite binary form.
The bits come out first-to-last from the top, so read the column downward: 0.625 = (0.101)₂ = 1/2 + 1/8.

epi-highlight.title: Essential prime implicants from the 1s covered only once
epi-highlight.intro: Σm(1, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D).

elements.text: Essential prime implicants: 1s with only one way out

steps.caption: f = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14) has 7 prime implicants. Count, for every 1-cell, how many of them contain it.
Three 1s lie in exactly one prime implicant: m1, m10 and m13 (shaded). Any cover must use that implicant, so it is essential.
The essential prime implicants: A′B′D, ACD′, ABC′. Draw them first.
Still uncovered: m6 and m7. Of the remaining prime implicants, A′BC covers both; A′CD or BCD′ would cover only one each and need a second term. So A′BC is the cheapest way to finish.
Minimal SOP: f = A′B′D + A′BC + ACD′ + ABC′. ABD′ is redundant: its 1s are all inside the essential ones.

equation-sieve.title: A system of Boolean equations solved by elimination
equation-sieve.intro: All 16 assignments of P, Q, R, S (row PQRS). Each equation keeps only the rows on which its two sides are equal.

elements.text: Solving a system by striking out rows

steps.caption: Equation: P + Q = 1. At least one of P, Q is 1: the four rows with P = Q = 0 go. Twelve rows survive.
Equation: PQ = 0. P and Q are not both 1: the four rows with P = Q = 1 go. Exactly one of P, Q is 1 on the eight survivors.
Equation: Q + R = R. Q + R = R means Q = 1 forces R = 1: rows 0100 and 0101 go. Six rows survive.
Equation: P′R + S = 0. A sum equal to 0: S = 0, and P = 0 forces R = 0, which kills the remaining P = 0 rows. Two rows survive: PQRS = 1000 and 1010.

excess3-correction.title: Excess-3 addition and its ±3 correction
excess3-correction.intro: 47 and 38 in excess-3 (each digit plus 3, in 4 bits).

elements.text: Excess-3 addition 47 + 38: −3 without a carry, +3 with one

steps.caption: Units: 1010 + 1011 = 1 0101. A carry came out, so the digit sum was 10 or more: add 3. 0101 + 0011 = 1000 (excess-3 of 5), decimal carry 1.
Tens: 0111 + 0110 + carry 1 = 1110, with no carry out: the digit sum was at most 9, so subtract 3: 1110 − 0011 = 1011 (excess-3 of 8).
Why: each code carries an excess of 3, so a sum carries an excess of 6. Without a carry, remove 3 to leave a single excess of 3. With a carry, the 16 taken away already over-removed, so put 3 back.
Result 1011 1000 is excess-3 of 85 = 47 + 38.

five-var-map.title: A five-variable K-map as two four-variable maps
five-var-map.intro: f(A, B, C, D, E) = Σm(0, 2, 7, 8, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 18, 24, 26, 27, 30, 31), drawn as an A = 0 map and an A = 1 map (rows B C, columns D E).

elements.text: Five variables: two 4-variable maps, A = 0 and A = 1

steps.caption: A 5-variable map is two 4-variable maps (rows B C, columns D E), one for A = 0 and one for A = 1. Inside each map the usual neighbours apply; in addition every cell is adjacent to the cell in the same position of the other map (they differ only in A).

set.text: same position in the other map = neighbour

steps.caption: The four corner cells of each map (C = 0, E = 0) are 1s in both maps. In each map they form a corner quad, and the two quads face each other: one group of 8 = 2³ cells, so 5 − 3 = 2 literals: C′E′.
Rows B C = 11 and 10, columns D E = 11 and 10 (B = 1, D = 1) are 1s in both maps: another octet across the maps, BD.
Remaining: m7 (00111) in the A = 0 map only. Its twin m23 is 0, so the loop cannot cross to A = 1; inside its own map it pairs with m15: A′CDE (4 literals).

set.text: twin cell is 0: the pair stays in one map

fixed-point-bits.title: Bit weights in a 5.3 fixed-point byte
fixed-point-bits.intro: Eight bit cells b7 to b0 with the binary point between b3 and b2. Weights above the point are 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; below it ½, ¼, ⅛. The pattern 01011.010 is 8 + 2 + 1 + ¼ = 11.25. The format covers 0 to 31.875 in steps of ⅛.

elements.text: Unsigned 5.3 fixed point: b₇ … b₃ . b₂ b₁ b₀
range 0 … 31.875 in steps of ⅛ (2⁸ = 256 values)

fixed-point-ruler.title: Fixed point: the range–resolution trade-off
fixed-point-ruler.intro: A number line from 0 to 16 with sixteen tick marks, one for each 4-bit pattern. Each step moves the binary point one place left.

elements.text: 4 bits, point moved: range shrinks, steps get finer

steps.caption: With 0 fraction bits (4.0 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 1 from 0 to 15: resolution 1, largest value 15 = 2⁴ − 1.
With 1 fraction bit (3.1 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.5 from 0 to 7.5: resolution 0.5, largest value 7.5 = 2³ − 0.5.
With 2 fraction bits (2.2 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.25 from 0 to 3.75: resolution 0.25, largest value 3.75 = 2² − 0.25.
With 3 fraction bits (1.3 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.125 from 0 to 1.875: resolution 0.125, largest value 1.875 = 2¹ − 0.125.
The count of values never changes: n bits always give 2ⁿ = 16 patterns. Moving the point only trades range for resolution.

fp-align-add.title: Floating-point addition: align, add, normalise, round
fp-align-add.intro: Two numbers in a toy format with 4 fraction bits: A = 7 = 1.1100 × 2² and B = 1.625 = 1.1010 × 2⁰.

steps.caption: Write both significands with their hidden 1 and two extra guard positions. A = 1.1100 × 2², B = 1.1010 × 2⁰. The exponents differ by 2.
Align: shift the smaller number right by 2 and raise its exponent to 2. B becomes 0.0110 × 2², and the bits shifted out (1 0) land in the guard and round positions instead of being lost.
Add the aligned significands: 1.1100 00 + 0.0110 10 = 10.0010 10. The sum overflowed into a second integer bit.
Normalise: 10.0010 10 has two bits before the point, so shift right by 1 and add 1 to the exponent: 1.0001 010 × 2³. The bit shifted out joins the extra bits: G = 0, R = 1.
Round to nearest even: the guard bit is 0, so the extra bits are less than half an ulp and are dropped. Result 1.0001 × 2³ = 8.5.

set.text: stored 8.5; exact sum 8.625 (error 0.125, under half an ulp = 0.25)

function-count.title: Counting Boolean functions: one free output bit per row
function-count.intro: A Boolean function is completely described by its output column. Count the columns.

elements.text: How many Boolean functions of n variables?

steps.caption: One variable: 2 rows. Each row's output is an independent choice of 0 or 1, so there are 2 × 2 = 2² = 4 functions: 0, x, x′ and 1.

set.text: a function = one output bit per row

steps.caption: Two variables: 4 rows, so 2⁴ = 16 functions, the sixteen of Lesson 1.
Three variables: 8 rows, so 2⁸ = 256 functions. In general n variables give 2ⁿ rows and 2^(2ⁿ) functions; for n = 4 that is 65 536.

gate-symbols.title: The seven logic gates with their truth tables filling row by row
gate-symbols.intro: NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR, each fed by the inputs A and B (NOT reads only A). The strip under each gate will hold its output for rows 00, 01, 10 and 11.

elements.text: The seven gates, row by row
The seven gates, row by row

steps.caption: Row 0: A = 0, B = 0. Outputs: NOT 1, AND 0, OR 0, NAND 1, NOR 1, XOR 0, XNOR 1.
Row 1: A = 0, B = 1. Outputs: NOT 1, AND 0, OR 1, NAND 1, NOR 0, XOR 1, XNOR 0.
Row 2: A = 1, B = 0. Outputs: NOT 0, AND 0, OR 1, NAND 1, NOR 0, XOR 1, XNOR 0.
Row 3: A = 1, B = 1. Outputs: NOT 0, AND 1, OR 1, NAND 0, NOR 0, XOR 0, XNOR 1.
Each gate's four outputs, read top to bottom, are its truth table: NOT 1100 (it reads only A), AND 0001, OR 0111, NAND 1110, NOR 1000, XOR 0110, XNOR 1001.

glitch-timing.title: Timing diagram of the X·X′ glitch
glitch-timing.intro: A signal X feeds an AND gate directly and through an inverter with a delay of 1 time unit. The AND gate is ideal (no delay).

elements.text: A glitch from a slow inverter: Y = X·X′

steps.caption: X rises at t = 2 and falls at t = 6. Logically Y = X·X′ is always 0.
The inverter takes one time unit, so X′ falls only at t = 3 and rises only at t = 7.
Between t = 2 and t = 3 both AND inputs are 1, so Y pulses to 1 for exactly the inverter delay: a static-0 hazard (a glitch).

set.text: 1-pulse of width = inverter delay on the rising edge

steps.caption: On the falling edge (t = 6 to 7) X is already 0 while X′ is still 0, so the AND sees 0, 0 and Y stays 0. The glitch appears only after X rises.

set.text: no glitch on the falling edge

gradual-underflow.title: Gradual underflow: denormals fill the hole around zero
gradual-underflow.intro: The values from 0 to 1 of a toy IEEE-style format with a 3-bit exponent (bias 3) and 2 fraction bits. At first only the normal numbers are drawn.

elements.text: A toy float (3-bit exponent, 2 fraction bits) between 0 and 1

steps.caption: With normal numbers only, the smallest positive value is 1/4 (1.00 × 2⁻²) and the next one down is 0. Just above 1/4 the values are 1/16 apart, but below it there is a hole four times wider.
Take x = 5/16 and y = 4/16, two different normal numbers. Their difference 1/16 falls in the hole, so a flush-to-zero machine returns x − y = 0 even though x ≠ y.
Denormals use the exponent field 0 with no hidden 1: 0.f × 2⁻², giving 1/16, 2/16 and 3/16. They fill the hole with the same 1/16 spacing as the first normal binade.

set.label: with denormals: evenly spaced down to 0

steps.caption: Now x − y = 1/16 is the denormal 0.01 × 2⁻², stored exactly. With denormals, x ≠ y always gives x − y ≠ 0.
The largest denormal, 3/16, is exactly one step below the smallest normal, 1/4. In IEEE single precision the same picture holds with 2⁻¹⁴⁹ steps up to 2⁻¹²⁶.

gray-reflect.title: Reflected Gray code, built by mirroring
gray-reflect.intro: The 1-bit Gray code, 0 and 1. Longer codes will be built to its right, each from the one before.

steps.caption: Start with the 1-bit Gray code: 0, 1. The two codes differ in one bit.
Copy the list, then append its mirror image (1, 0) underneath. Put 0 in front of the top half and 1 in front of the bottom half: 00, 01, 11, 10.
Do it again: the 2-bit list, then its mirror, with prefixes 0 and 1. The result is the 3-bit reflected Gray code: 000 001 011 010 110 111 101 100.
Across the mirror line the two neighbours are the same code with only the new front bit changed (010 → 110). And the last code 100 differs from the first 000 in one bit too, so the list wraps round.

gray-wheel.title: Rotary encoder disc in Gray code
gray-wheel.intro: A disc cut into 8 sectors and 3 rings. Reading clockwise from the top, the sectors are coded 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100. At every boundary between neighbouring sectors only one ring changes between clear and shaded, so a sensor sitting on a boundary can misread at most one bit and is never more than one position wrong.

elements.text: inner ring = first bit, outer ring = last bit; shaded = 1

gray-xor-ladder.title: The XOR ladder between binary and Gray
gray-xor-ladder.intro: The binary number 1011 on top and an empty Gray row underneath.

elements.text: Binary → Gray: XOR each bit with its left neighbour

steps.caption: The first Gray bit is the first binary bit, copied: 1.
The second Gray bit (from the left) = first binary bit ⊕ second binary bit = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
The third Gray bit (from the left) = second binary bit ⊕ third binary bit = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
The fourth Gray bit (from the left) = third binary bit ⊕ fourth binary bit = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
So binary 1011 (eleven) has Gray code 1110. In one line: Gray = b ⊕ (b shifted right by 1).
Going back, each binary bit is the XOR of all Gray bits from the left down to it, a running XOR: Gray 101100 gives binary 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1 = 110111.

grouping-slider.title: Grouping bits into octal and hex digits
grouping-slider.intro: The seven bits 1011010. The red dot marks the radix point at the right end. Dashed cells on the left are padding zeros that will appear when a group runs short.

elements.text: Grouping the bits of (1011010)₂ from the right

steps.caption: Start at the radix point (here, just right of the last bit) and cut off three bits: 010. Three bits make one octal digit, and 010 is 2.
The next three bits to the left, 011, are the octal digit 3.
Only one bit, 1, is left. Pad it on the left with two zeros (that adds nothing to the value) to make 001 = 1.
Read the groups left to right: (1011010)₂ = (132)₈. Check: 64 + 24 + 2 = 90.
Now regroup in fours for hexadecimal, again starting at the point: 1010 is A.
The last three bits 101 need one padding zero: 0101 = 5. So (1011010)₂ = (5A)₁₆ = 5·16 + 10 = 90.

hamming-74-venn.title: Hamming (7,4) as three overlapping parity circles
hamming-74-venn.intro: Three overlapping circles named 1, 2 and 4. The seven regions hold bit positions 1 to 7: position 7 is in all three circles, 3 in circles 1 and 2, 5 in circles 1 and 4, 6 in circles 2 and 4, and 1, 2, 4 each in one circle only. The data bits 1, 0, 1, 1 sit in positions 3, 5, 6, 7.

steps.caption: Each parity bit makes its circle hold an even number of 1s. Circle 1 holds positions 3, 5, 7 = 1, 0, 1: two 1s already, so p1 = 0.
Circle 2 holds positions 3, 6, 7 = 1, 1, 1: three 1s, so p2 = 1 to make four.
Circle 4 holds positions 5, 6, 7 = 0, 1, 1: two 1s, so p4 = 0. The codeword (positions 1–7) is 0110011.
Noise flips position 6 (1 → 0). The received word is 0110001.
Recount each circle. Circle 1 is still even (it does not contain position 6). Circles 2 and 4 are now odd: they fail.
Add the numbers of the failing circles: 2 + 4 = 6. The only position inside circles 2 and 4 but outside circle 1 is 6, so flip it back. Syndrome 6, corrected word 0110011.

hazard-glitch.title: A static-1 hazard in AB + A′C and the consensus term that removes it
hazard-glitch.intro: f = AB + A′C built as AND–OR with an inverter on A (delay 1); B and C are held at 1 while A falls at t = 3.

elements.text: A static-1 hazard and the consensus fix

steps.caption: f = AB + A′C with B = C = 1, so logically f = A + A′ = 1 whatever A does. A falls at t = 3; the inverter makes A′ rise one unit later, at t = 4.
AB follows A and falls at t = 3; A′C follows A′ and rises only at t = 4. For one time unit both AND outputs are 0.
So f = AB + A′C drops to 0 between t = 3 and t = 4: a static-1 hazard. On the map the two 1-cells m7 (A = 1) and m3 (A = 0) are adjacent but lie in different loops.
Add the consensus term BC, the loop that contains both m3 and m7. With B = C = 1 it is 1 throughout, so f = AB + A′C + BC stays 1: the hazard is gone, at the cost of one more AND gate.

set.text: add BC: every adjacent pair of 1s now shares a loop

hex-nibble-table.title: The sixteen hex digits as 4-bit groups, with their count of 1s
hex-nibble-table.intro: Two tables. Left: hex digits 0 to 7, right: 8 to F. Each row gives the digit, its four bits, how many of those bits are 1, and its decimal value. For example 7 is 0111 with three 1s, and F is 1111 with four 1s.

horner-chain.title: Horner's chain: (257)₈ to decimal
horner-chain.intro: Start with a running total of 0. Each arrow will multiply the total by the base 8 and add one digit.

elements.text: Horner's chain for (257)₈: multiply by 8, add the next digit

steps.caption: Take the running total 0, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 2: 0 × 8 + 2 = 2.
Take the running total 2, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 5: 2 × 8 + 5 = 21.
Take the running total 21, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 7: 21 × 8 + 7 = 175.
Every digit has been used, so the last total is the value: (257)₈ = 175. The same total comes from 2·64 + 5·8 + 7, but without writing any powers.

ieee-encode.title: Decimal to IEEE-754: encoding 13.625
ieee-encode.intro: We will turn 13.625 into a 32-bit single-precision word, one decision at a time.

steps.caption: Step 1, the sign: 13.625 is positive, so the sign bit is 0.
Step 2, the integer part in binary: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 1101₂.
Step 3, the fraction part by repeated doubling: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25 (bit 1), 0.25 × 2 = 0.5 (bit 0), 0.5 × 2 = 1.0 (bit 1). So 0.625 = 0.101₂, and it terminates.
Step 4, normalise: move the point 3 places left so exactly one 1 is before it. 1101.101₂ = 1.101101₂ × 2³.
Step 5, bias the exponent: e = 3 + 127 = 130 = 10000010₂.
Step 6, the fraction field holds the bits after the point (the leading 1 is hidden): 101101, padded with 17 zeros to 23 bits.
Step 7, assemble sign | exponent | fraction into 32 bits.
Step 8, regroup the 32 bits in fours to get hex: 0x415A0000. Decoding it gives 1.703125 × 8 = 13.625 exactly, because 13.625 = 109/8 has a power-of-two denominator.

ieee-layout.title: IEEE-754 single and double layouts
ieee-layout.intro: The 32 bits of −6.75 in single precision, split into a 1-bit sign (red), an 8-bit exponent (blue) and a 23-bit fraction (green).

elements.text: IEEE-754 layouts: −6.75 in single, then in double

steps.caption: The sign bit (bit 31) comes first. It is 1, so the number is negative. The significand is stored as a magnitude: sign-magnitude, not 2's complement.
Bits 30–23 hold the biased exponent e = 10000001 = 129. Subtracting the bias 127 gives the true exponent E = 2.
Bits 22–0 hold the fraction f = 1011 followed by zeros. The leading 1 of the significand is hidden, so the significand is 1.1011₂ = 1.6875.
Put it together: (−1)¹ × 1.1011₂ × 2² = −110.11₂ = −6.75. In hex the word is 0xC0D80000.
Double precision keeps the same three fields, only wider: 1 sign bit, an 11-bit exponent with bias 1023, and a 52-bit fraction.
The same −6.75 as a double: the true exponent is still 2, so e = 1025; the fraction 1011 is padded with 48 zeros. The word is 0xC01B000000000000.

ieee-special-values.title: IEEE-754 special values
ieee-special-values.intro: The five ways IEEE-754 single precision reads a word, chosen by the exponent field and whether the fraction is zero.

elements.text: How IEEE-754 single precision reads the exponent field

steps.caption: 0x00000000 is +0 and 0x80000000 is −0. They compare equal, but 1/(+0) = +∞ and 1/(−0) = −∞.
0x00400000 has e = 0 and f = 100…0: a denormal, 0.1₂ × 2⁻¹²⁶ = 2⁻¹²⁷. No hidden 1, and the exponent is fixed at −126.
Every field from 1 to 254 is an ordinary number with a hidden 1: 0x3F800000 has e = 127, so it is 1.0.
0x7F800000 is +∞ and 0xFF800000 is −∞: the results of overflow or of dividing a non-zero number by zero.
0x7FC00000 has e = 255 and a non-zero fraction: NaN, from 0/0, ∞ − ∞ or √−1. NaN is unequal even to itself.
Only the two end fields are special. The 254 fields in between hold every normal number, from 2⁻¹²⁶ up to about 3.4 × 10³⁸.

kmap-adjacency.title: Neighbours of a cell on a 4-variable K-map, through the edges too
kmap-adjacency.intro: A 4-variable map with every cell numbered (rows A B, columns C D).

elements.text: Neighbours on a K-map, edges included

steps.caption: m5 = 0101. Its four neighbours are the cells above, below, left and right: m1, m4, m7, m13. Each differs from 0101 in exactly one bit.
m8 = 1000 sits on the bottom-left corner. Its neighbours are m10 (right edge, through the wrap), m0 (top row, through the wrap), m9 and m12: still exactly one bit different each.
m2 = 0010 is in the top row, last column. Its neighbours: m0 (left end of the same row, through the wrap), m3, m6 and m10 (bottom row, through the wrap).

set.text: roll the map: left meets right

steps.caption: Picture the map rolled into a tube (left edge glued to right) and the tube bent into a ring (top glued to bottom): a torus. On that surface every cell has exactly four neighbours, and they are exactly the minterms one bit away.

kmap-checkerboard.title: The checkerboard K-map of 4-variable parity
kmap-checkerboard.intro: A 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D) with 1s on the odd-parity minterms.

elements.text: The checkerboard: parity cannot be grouped

steps.caption: The 1s are the minterms with an odd number of 1 bits: 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14. They form a checkerboard.
Every neighbour of a 1 is a 0: moving to a neighbour flips one bit, which changes the parity. Here m1 = 0001 and its neighbours m0, m3, m5, m9 all have an even number of 1s.

set.text: each neighbour flips one bit → parity flips

steps.caption: So no two 1s are adjacent: every prime implicant is a single minterm, and the minimal SOP has all 8 minterms (32 literals). The compact form is the XOR A ⊕ B ⊕ C ⊕ D.
A partial checkerboard, where only some variables alternate, does group: 1s where B = D form the two quads B′D′ (corners) and BD (centre), so f = B′D′ + BD = (B ⊕ D)′.

kmap-corner-quad.title: The corner quad B′D′ on a 4-variable K-map
kmap-corner-quad.intro: A 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D) with 1s in the four corner cells.

elements.text: The four corners form one group
The four corners are one group

steps.caption: The 1s are the four corners: m0 = 0000, m2 = 0010, m8 = 1000, m10 = 1010. They look as far apart as cells can be.
Across the left/right edge: m0 and m2 differ only in C (0000, 0010), and so do m8 and m10. Across the top/bottom edge: m0 and m8 differ only in A, m2 and m10 too.
So the four corners are a 2 × 2 block on the torus: one group of 4, drawn as four corner pieces that reach outward through the edges.
Inside the group A and C both change; B = 0 and D = 0 never change. A group of 4 = 2² cells keeps 4 − 2 = 2 literals: B′D′.

set.text: A and C change: they drop

kmap-gray-layout.title: Placing minterms on a 4-variable K-map in Gray order
kmap-gray-layout.intro: An empty 4-variable map. Rows will be labelled by A B and columns by C D. Minterm m has A as its most significant bit.

steps.caption: Columns are labelled by C D and rows by A B, each in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10: the third label is 11, not 10, so that every step along an axis flips exactly one bit.
Row A B = 00: minterm number = 4·(A B) + (C D), so the row reads 0, 1, 3, 2. The last two are swapped compared with counting order, because the columns are in Gray order.
Row A B = 01: minterm number = 4·(A B) + (C D), so the row reads 4, 5, 7, 6. The last two are swapped compared with counting order, because the columns are in Gray order.
Row A B = 11: minterm number = 4·(A B) + (C D), so the row reads 12, 13, 15, 14. The last two are swapped compared with counting order, because the columns are in Gray order.
Row A B = 10: minterm number = 4·(A B) + (C D), so the row reads 8, 9, 11, 10. The last two are swapped compared with counting order, because the columns are in Gray order.
The finished map, cell numbers 0 1 3 2 / 4 5 7 6 / 12 13 15 14 / 8 9 11 10. Any two cells side by side (or at opposite ends of a row or column) differ in exactly one variable.

set.text: Memorise the pattern: swap the last two of every row, then the last two rows.

kmap-grouping.title: Grouping a 4-variable K-map: an octet and two wrap-around quads
kmap-grouping.intro: Σm(0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D).

elements.text: Grouping the 1s: biggest legal loops, fewest of them

steps.caption: Eleven 1s to cover. Look for the largest possible groups first, but make sure every loop is a rectangle of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells (wrap-around allowed).
The first two columns (C D = 00 and 01) are all 1s: an octet. C is 0 in both columns; A, B and D all change. 8 = 2³ cells keep 4 − 3 = 1 literal: C′.

Still uncovered: m2, m6 and m14 (column C D = 10). Start with m2 and m6: they join m0 and m4 in the first column through the left/right wrap: a quad in rows A B = 00, 01. A = 0 and D = 0 stay fixed: A′D′.
Still uncovered: m14. Its biggest loop also wraps: m12, m14 with m4, m6 in rows A B = 01, 11. B = 1 and D = 0 stay fixed: BD′.
Every 1 is now inside a loop, and no loop can be bigger or dropped. Minimal SOP: f = C′ + A′D′ + BD′, with 5 literals.

kmap-pos-zeros.title: Minimal POS by grouping the 0s of a K-map
kmap-pos-zeros.intro: F(P, Q, R, S) = PQ + P′QR + P′QR′S on a map with rows P Q and columns R S; the 0s are shown.

elements.text: POS: loop the 0s, read sum terms

steps.caption: F = PQ + P′QR + P′QR′S has 9 zeros: m0, m1, m2, m3, m4, m8, m9, m10, m11. For a product of sums, loop the 0s exactly as you would loop 1s.
Rows P Q = 00 and 10 are all 0s: an octet of 0s. Q = 0 throughout. A group of 0s is read as a sum term with each fixed variable written so that it is 0 on the group: Q = 0 gives the factor (Q).
Left: m4 = 0100. Pair it with m0 (column R S = 00, rows 00 and 01): P = 0, R = 0, S = 0 are fixed, so the factor is (P + R + S) (a 0 bit gives the plain letter).
Minimal POS: F = (Q)(P + R + S), 4 literals. The minimal SOP, QS + QR + PQ, needs 6. Here the POS is cheaper.

kmap-trap-labels.title: A K-map printed with binary-order labels, re-drawn in Gray order
kmap-trap-labels.intro: A 3-variable map with rows A = 0, 1 and columns labelled B C = 00, 01, 10, 11 as printed in a GATE paper. Each row reads 1 0 0 1.

elements.text: Trap: a map printed in binary order

steps.caption: The columns are labelled 00, 01, 10, 11: plain counting order, not Gray order. Between the 2nd and 3rd columns two bits change (01 → 10), and the two end columns (00 and 11) are not neighbours either.
The tempting mistake: treat the end columns as a wrap-around group of four 1s and write C′. On this map the ends differ in two bits, so that loop is illegal.

set.text: wrap loop of the ends: illegal

steps.caption: Re-draw the columns in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10: the column of 1s labelled 11 moves to the third place. Now the 1s are in columns 00 and 11, which are not adjacent.
Two vertical pairs: B = C = 0 gives B′C′, B = C = 1 gives BC (A changes in both, so it drops). f = B′C′ + BC = (B ⊕ C)′, the XNOR of B and C.

law-cards.title: Proving Boolean laws by truth table
law-cards.intro: Three laws, each proved by listing every case: idempotence, absorption, and the redundant-literal rule.

steps.caption: Card 1. Idempotence: x + x = x and x·x = x: list every row of the variables (2 rows).

set.text: Idempotence: x + x = x and x·x = x

steps.caption: Fill each column from the definitions. The highlighted columns x, x+x, xx agree on every row. With only 2 possible rows, that is a complete proof.
Card 2. Absorption: x + xy = x: list every row of the variables (4 rows).
Fill each column from the definitions. The highlighted columns x, x+xy agree on every row. With only 4 possible rows, that is a complete proof.
Card 3. Redundant literal: x + x′y = x + y: list every row of the variables (4 rows).

set.text: Redundant literal: x + x′y = x + y

steps.caption: Fill each column from the definitions. The highlighted columns x+x′y, x+y agree on every row. With only 4 possible rows, that is a complete proof.

minterm-highlighter.title: Expanding a sum of products into its minterms
minterm-highlighter.intro: f(P, Q, R) = PQ + QR′ + PR′. The rows are numbered with P as the most significant bit.

elements.text: From terms to minterms: each term lights its rows

steps.caption: The term PQ fixes 2 of the 3 variables, so it covers 2 rows: 110, 111, that is minterms 6 and 7.
The term QR′ fixes 2 of the 3 variables, so it covers 2 rows: 010, 110, that is minterms 2 and 6.
The term PR′ fixes 2 of the 3 variables, so it covers 2 rows: 100, 110, that is minterms 4 and 6.
f is the OR of the three columns: it is 1 wherever at least one term is 1. Row 6 is covered three times but is counted once.
Read the 1-rows of f: the canonical sum of products is Σm(2, 4, 6, 7), and the remaining rows give the product of maxterms ΠM(0, 1, 3, 5).

minterm-set-venn.title: AND, OR, XOR and NOT as set operations on minterm lists
minterm-set-venn.intro: Two functions of three variables, f = Σ(1, 3, 5, 7) and g = Σ(3, 6, 7), each drawn as the set of rows where it is 1.

steps.caption: AND keeps the rows that are in both sets: f·g = Σ(3, 7) (intersection).
OR keeps the rows in either set: f + g = Σ(1, 3, 5, 6, 7) (union).
XOR keeps the rows in exactly one set: f ⊕ g = Σ(1, 5, 6) (symmetric difference).
NOT keeps the rows outside the set: f′ = Σ(0, 2, 4, 6) (complement).

msb-weight-bar.title: Place values of an 8-bit 2's-complement number
msb-weight-bar.intro: Eight bit cells with weights −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; the leftmost weight is negative. The pattern 10110100 has 1s under −128, 32, 16 and 4, so it is worth −76. The range is −128 to +127.

multi-output-sharing.title: Two outputs sharing a product term
multi-output-sharing.intro: Two functions of A, B, C to be built together; each map has rows A and columns B C.

elements.text: Two outputs, one shared product term

steps.caption: Minimise each output alone: f₁ = A′C + BC and f₂ = AB + BC. Built separately that is 4 AND gates (8 inputs) and 2 OR gates (4 inputs).
BC (m3, m7) appears in both answers. Build that AND gate once and send its output to both OR gates.

set.text: share BC: one gate, two fan-outs

steps.caption: Shared: 3 AND gates and 2 OR gates, 10 gate inputs. In multi-output design, look for product terms that can serve several outputs (Lesson 4 also shows a case where the shared term is not prime for either output).

set.text: f₁ = A′C + BC,  f₂ = AB + BC: 3 ANDs

nand-builds.title: Building NOT, AND and OR from NAND gates
nand-builds.intro: NAND gates only. Three small circuits will appear, one per basic gate.

elements.text: Everything from NAND: NOT, AND and OR

steps.caption: NOT: tie both inputs of a NAND together. NAND(x, x) = (x·x)′ = x′. One gate.
AND: a NAND followed by a NAND used as an inverter undoes the inversion: ((AB)′)′ = AB. Two gates.
OR: invert both inputs, then NAND them: (A′·B′)′ = A + B by De Morgan. Three gates.
NOT, AND and OR can build every function (canonical SOP), so NAND alone can build every function: it is universal. The NOR gate is the dual: NOT 1, OR 2, AND 3.

nand-nand-conversion.title: Converting AND–OR into NAND–NAND
nand-nand-conversion.intro: A sum of products, F = AB + CD, built as AND gates feeding an OR gate.

elements.text: AND–OR to NAND–NAND by bubble pairs

steps.caption: Start from the two-level AND–OR circuit for F = AB + CD: one AND per product term, one OR to combine them.
Put a bubble at the output of each AND and a bubble at the matching OR input. Each wire now has two bubbles, which cancel, so the function is unchanged.
An OR with bubbled inputs is a NAND (De Morgan). Redraw it: the whole circuit is now NAND–NAND.
Rule: any two-level AND–OR (sum of products) becomes NAND–NAND by replacing every gate with a NAND. A single-literal term must first pass through an inverter.

nand-nand-from-kmap.title: From a minimal SOP to a NAND–NAND circuit
nand-nand-from-kmap.intro: f(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7) on a 3-variable map (rows A, columns B C); complemented inputs are available.

elements.text: From a K-map to a NAND–NAND circuit

steps.caption: Loop the map: A′C (m1, m3) and AB (m6, m7). The minimal SOP is f = A′C + AB.
Each loop becomes an AND gate fed by its literals (A′ is available as an input), and the OR gate collects the loops: a two-level AND–OR circuit.

set.text: loops → AND gates, sum → OR gate

steps.caption: Put two bubbles on each wire between the levels (a double inversion changes nothing). An AND with an output bubble is a NAND; an OR with input bubbles is, by De Morgan, a NAND.

set.text: add bubble pairs on the middle wires

steps.caption: So the same circuit is three NAND gates: f = NAND(NAND(A′, C), NAND(A, B)). Every SOP becomes NAND–NAND this way; a POS becomes NOR–NOR dually.

negate-invert-plus-one.title: Invert and add 1, and the copy-to-the-first-1 shortcut
negate-invert-plus-one.intro: The 8-bit pattern of +88: 01011000. We will build the pattern of −88 underneath.

elements.text: Negating +88 in 8 bits: invert, then add 1

steps.caption: Flip every bit of 01011000. The result 10100111 is x̄, and x + x̄ = 11111111 = 2⁸ − 1.
Add 1 to x̄. The three trailing 1s of x̄ turn into 0s as the carry ripples left, and the first 0 it meets becomes 1.
Compare x and −x: the rightmost 1 of x and everything to its right (1000) are copied unchanged; every bit to its left is flipped. That is the copy-to-the-first-1 shortcut.
Check: 10101000 read with the −128 weight is −128 + 32 + 8 = −88.

normalise-shift.title: Normalising a significand: shift left, lower the exponent
normalise-shift.intro: The significand 0.0001011 times 2 to the 6 is 5.5, but it starts with three zeros after the point, which waste precision.

elements.label: not normalised: three 0s after the point

steps.caption: Find the first 1. It sits in the 4th place after the point, so the significand starts with three wasted zeros.
Fraction form (0.1…): shift the significand 3 places left, so the first 1 sits just after the point. A left shift by 3 multiplies by 2³, so the exponent drops by 3: 0.1011 × 2³.
Hidden-bit form (1.f): shift one more place, so the first 1 sits before the point. The exponent drops once more: 1.011 × 2².
In the hidden-bit form the bit before the point is always 1, so it is not stored. The fraction field keeps only 011 (then zeros), and every shift kept the value at 5.5.

octal-hex-bridge.title: The binary bridge from octal to hex
octal-hex-bridge.intro: The octal numeral 546, one box per digit. Binary and hex rows will appear under it.

elements.text: Octal → binary → hexadecimal, never through decimal

steps.caption: Write each octal digit as exactly three bits: 5 → 101, 4 → 100, 6 → 110. Each digit is replaced on its own; nothing carries between digits.
Now forget the old boundaries. Cut the bit string into fours, starting from the right end (the radix point).
The leftmost group has only one bit, so pad it with three zeros on the left: 0001.
Read each four-bit group as one hex digit: 0001 → 1, 0110 → 6, 0110 → 6.

odometer-rollover.title: An odometer that rolls over at 3
odometer-rollover.intro: Four counter wheels, all at 0. Under each wheel is the place value it stands for: 27, 9, 3 and 1.

elements.text: A base-3 counter (each wheel shows 0, 1 or 2)

steps.caption: One count: the right wheel moves from 0 to 1.
Two counts: the right wheel shows 2, the largest digit base 3 allows.
Three counts: the right wheel cannot show 3, so it rolls back to 0 and pushes the next wheel on by one. The display reads 10, which in base 3 means one three and no ones.
Jump ahead to 26 counts: the three right-hand wheels all show their largest digit, 0222. That is 2·9 + 2·3 + 2 = 26 = 3³ − 1.
One more count rolls each of those three wheels over to 0 in turn, and the carry ripples into the fourth wheel: 1000 in base 3 is 3³ = 27. In any base, 1 followed by k zeros is b to the power k.

overflow-carries.title: Overflow and the carries of the sign column
overflow-carries.intro: Three 4-bit 2's-complement additions. Above the sign column we show the carry into it (c₃) and out of it (c₄).

elements.text: Overflow: compare the carry into and out of the sign bit
Carry in vs carry out of the MSB

steps.caption: +5 + (+4): 0101 + 0100 = 0 1001. Carry into the sign column c₃ = 1, carry out c₄ = 0. They differ, so overflow (true sum 9 is outside −8 … 7).
−5 + (−6): 1011 + 1010 = 1 0101. Carry into the sign column c₃ = 0, carry out c₄ = 1. They differ, so overflow (true sum −11 is outside −8 … 7).
+5 + (−3): 0101 + 1101 = 1 0010. Carry into the sign column c₃ = 1, carry out c₄ = 1. They agree, so no overflow (the sum 2 fits). The carry out alone is not overflow.
Rule: V = c₃ ⊕ c₄. Equivalently, overflow happens exactly when both operands have the same sign and the result's sign differs.

set.text: V = carry in ⊕ carry out (sign column)

overflow-wheel.title: Overflow on the 2's-complement wheel
overflow-wheel.intro: The 4-bit wheel with 2's-complement values inside. The green band marks the non-negative patterns, the red band the negative ones; they meet at the seam between 0111 (+7) and 1000 (−8).

elements.text: Adding on the wheel: overflow is crossing the seam

steps.caption: Start at 0101 = +5. Adding a positive number means stepping clockwise.
Add +4: four steps clockwise pass 0111 (+7) and cross the seam into 1001. The pattern reads −7, but 5 + 4 = 9 does not fit in 4 bits. Overflow.
Start at 1010 = −6 and add −3: three steps anticlockwise cross the seam backwards to 0111 = +7. The true sum −9 is below −8. Overflow again.

Now 0101 (+5) + 1101 (−3). As unsigned steps that is 13 clockwise, which lands in the same place as 3 steps back (13 = 16 − 3): 0010 = +2. The band shows the short way round. The 13-step route only passes 0000 (a carry out of 4 bits, dropped); the seam is not crossed, so +2 is right.

Rule: a sum overflows exactly when it crosses the +7 / −8 seam. That can only happen when both operands have the same sign. (Chapter 5 turns this into a gate: carry into the sign bit ≠ carry out of it.)

pi-chart-dominance.title: A prime-implicant chart reduced by essential rows and row dominance
pi-chart-dominance.intro: f = Σm(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 14): its six prime implicants (rows) against its ten 1-cells (columns).

elements.text: The prime-implicant chart: essential rows, then dominance

steps.caption: Rows are the six prime implicants, columns the ten 1-cells; × means the PI covers that cell. A minimal SOP must pick rows so that every column has a × in a picked row.
Columns 9 and 14 contain a single ×: only B′C′ covers m9 and only CD′ covers m14. Both rows are essential.
Delete every column the essential rows cover (0, 1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 10, 14). Only columns 5 and 7 remain.

Row dominance: on the remaining columns A′BD covers {5, 7}, A′C′D only {5}, A′BC only {7}. A′BD dominates both (and costs no more), so the dominated rows are greyed out and their marks removed; B′D′ now covers nothing and is dropped too.

Minimal SOP: the two essential rows plus A′BD. (Column dominance gives the same result from the other side: column 9's only row, B′C′, also covers 0, 1 and 8, so those columns could have been dropped at once.)

pi-enumeration.title: Listing every prime implicant of a 4-variable function
pi-enumeration.intro: Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 14) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D).

steps.caption: f = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 14). A prime implicant is a loop that cannot be made any bigger. Grow a loop from every 1 in every direction it can go.
Starting from m0: the whole top row is 1s, a quad A′B′. It cannot grow (neither row A B = 01 nor row 10, its wrap-around neighbour, is all 1s).
Starting from m5: m1, m3, m5, m7 form a quad A′D (rows 00 and 01, columns 01 and 11).
Starting from m8: m0, m2, m8, m10 are the four corners, a quad B′D′.
Starting from m14: its only neighbouring 1 is m10, so the largest loop is the pair ACD′. Every 1 has now been a starting point and no new maximal loop appeared: there are exactly 4 prime implicants.
A prime implicant is not always needed: A′B′'s cells 0, 2 are inside B′D′ and 1, 3 inside A′D. It is a prime implicant but a redundant one. Minimal SOP: f = A′D + B′D′ + ACD′.

place-value-strip.title: Place value: the same digits in base 3 and base 5
place-value-strip.intro: The digits 1 2 0 1 in four cells. Above each cell is its place value in base 3, a power of 3 that grows from right to left.

steps.caption: The first digit is 1 and sits in the 3³ = 27 place, so it adds 1 × 27 = 27. Running total: 27.
The second digit is 2 and sits in the 3² = 9 place, so it adds 2 × 9 = 18. Running total: 45.
The third digit is 0 and sits in the 3¹ = 3 place, so it adds 0 × 3 = 0. Running total: 45.
The fourth digit is 1 and sits in the 3⁰ = 1 place, so it adds 1 × 1 = 1. Running total: 46. So (1201)₃ = 46.
Now keep the same four digits but switch the base to 5. Only the place values change: 125, 25, 5 and 1.
Weighting each digit again: 125 + 50 + 0 + 1 = 176. Same digits, larger base, larger value: (1201)₅ = 176.

pos-neg-logic.title: Positive and negative logic: one physical gate read two ways
pos-neg-logic.intro: A physical gate's behaviour in voltages: H is the high level, L the low level.

steps.caption: The datasheet lists only voltages. The output is H only when both inputs are H.
Read H as 1 and L as 0 (positive logic). F is 1 only on row 11: this gate is an AND.
Now read L as 1 and H as 0 (negative logic). Every 0 becomes 1 and vice versa, in the inputs and in the output.
Sort the negative-logic rows into the usual order 00, 01, 10, 11: F reads 0, 1, 1, 1. The same chip is an OR gate.
Changing the convention complements every input and the output, which turns each function into its dual: AND ↔ OR, NAND ↔ NOR, XOR ↔ XNOR.

qm-tabulation.title: Quine–McCluskey tabulation of Σm(0, 2, 4, 5, 6, 10)
qm-tabulation.intro: The tabular method needs no picture: list the minterms in binary and merge cubes that differ in one bit, round by round.

elements.text: Quine–McCluskey: combine neighbours in the table

steps.caption: List the minterms in binary, sorted by their number of 1s: group 0 = {0}, group 1 = {2, 4}, group 2 = {5, 6, 10}. Only neighbouring groups can combine, because a combinable pair differs in exactly one bit.

Compare group 0 with group 1: 0000 with 0010 gives 00-0, with 0100 gives 0-00. Compare group 1 with group 2: 0010 with 0110 → 0-10, with 1010 → -010; 0100 with 0101 → 010-, with 0110 → 01-0. Every minterm was used, so all get a tick.

Round 1 (pairs), grouped by their 1s: {00-0, 0-00} then {010-, 01-0, 0-10, -010}. Two pairs combine only if their dashes are in the same place and they differ in one other bit: 00-0 + 01-0 = 0--0, and 0-00 + 0-10 = 0--0 again (record it once).

Tick the pairs that combined (00-0, 0-00, 01-0, 0-10). 010- and -010 found no partner with matching dashes: they are prime implicants. Round 2 has a single cube, 0--0, which cannot combine further: also prime.
Prime implicants: 0--0 = A′D′, 010- = A′BC′, -010 = B′CD′. That is 3 PIs, the same answer the map gives (GATE 2015).

radix-solutions-grid.title: Counting radix solutions: every candidate pair, with the invalid ones explained
radix-solutions-grid.intro: Two tables of candidate pairs. A tick marks a pair that satisfies the equation and every digit limit. A cross names the rule the pair breaks: y = 1 is not a base, the digit 8 needs y ≥ 9, and the digit 4 needs x ≥ 5.

recurring-loop.title: Why 0.1 recurs in binary
recurring-loop.intro: The same doubling method as for 0.625, applied to 0.1. Watch the fraction that is kept after each row.

elements.text: 0.1 to binary never stops: the fraction comes back

steps.caption: The fraction left over is 0.2 again, the same as after the first row. From here the same four rows repeat for ever, so the bits 0011 repeat for ever.
So 0.1 = (0.0 0011 0011 0011 …)₂, a recurring binary fraction. Any finite number of bits only approximates it.

repeated-division-ladder.title: Repeated division: 2748 to hexadecimal
repeated-division-ladder.intro: We will divide by 16 again and again. Each remainder becomes one hex digit.

elements.text: Convert 2748 to base 16: divide by 16, keep the remainder

steps.caption: Divide 2748 by 16: quotient 171, remainder 12, which is written C in hex. This first remainder is the units digit.
Divide 171 by 16: quotient 10, remainder 11, which is written B in hex. Carry on with the quotient.
Divide 10 by 16: quotient 0, remainder 10, which is written A in hex. The quotient is now 0, so we stop.
The first remainder is the lowest digit and the last remainder is the leading digit, so read the column from the bottom up: A, B, C.

round-nearest-even.title: Round to nearest, ties to even
round-nearest-even.intro: A significand with 4 kept fraction bits, followed by the guard (G), round (R) and sticky (S) bits that the hardware keeps while it computes.

elements.text: Round to nearest, ties to even, from the G, R and S bits

steps.caption: Kept bits 1.0110, extra bits G R S = 0 1 1. G = 0: less than half an ulp, round down (truncate). Result 1.0110.
Kept bits 1.0110, extra bits G R S = 1 0 1. G = 1 and R or S = 1: more than half an ulp, round up. Result 1.0111.
Kept bits 1.0110, extra bits G R S = 1 0 0. G = 1, R = S = 0: exactly half. Tie: keep the even last bit (0), so round down. Result 1.0110.
Kept bits 1.0111, extra bits G R S = 1 0 0. Exactly half again, but the last kept bit is 1 (odd): round up to make it even. Result 1.1000.

set.text: Exactly half again, but the last kept bit is 1 (odd)

self-dual-pairs.title: The complementary-pair test for self-dual functions
self-dual-pairs.intro: The eight rows of a 3-variable truth table, arranged in complementary pairs.

elements.text: Self-dual: exactly one row of every complementary pair

steps.caption: Pair every row with its bitwise complement: (0, 7), (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4). The two indices always add up to 2ⁿ − 1 = 7.
f = Σ(0, 1, 2, 4) takes exactly one row from each pair (0 from the first, 1, 2 and 4 from the others). So f(x′) = f(x)′ on every row: f is self-dual.
g = Σ(0, 1, 6, 7) also has four minterms (it is neutral), but it takes both rows of the pairs (0, 7) and (1, 6) and none of the others. Not self-dual.
Counting: a self-dual function is one free choice per pair. There are 2ⁿ⁻¹ pairs, so 2^(2ⁿ⁻¹) self-dual functions: 2⁴ = 16 for n = 3.

shannon-tree.title: Shannon expansion as a decision tree
shannon-tree.intro: f = AB + A′C. Shannon expansion splits f on one variable into two smaller functions, the cofactors.

steps.caption: Set A = 0: the term AB vanishes and A′C becomes C. The cofactor is f(0, B, C) = C.
Set A = 1: the term A′C vanishes and AB becomes B. The cofactor is f(1, B, C) = B.
Glue the halves back, each with the literal that selects it: f = A′·C + A·B, which is f again.
Keep splitting and every path ends in a constant. This decision tree describes f completely; a 2:1 multiplexer is the same picture in hardware (Chapter 4).

sign-extension-stretch.title: Sign extension keeps the value
sign-extension-stretch.intro: The 4-bit pattern 1101 at the right. Wider copies of it will appear underneath, lined up on the right.

elements.text: Sign extension: copy the sign bit into every new place

steps.caption: −3 in 4 bits is 1101: the sign bit (weight −8) is 1.
To widen to 8 bits, copy the sign bit 1 into the four new places: 1111 1101. The value is still −3 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = −3).
Widen again to 16 bits: twelve copies of the sign bit in front of 1101. Still −3.
Padding with zeros instead (0000 1101) would give +13: zero-padding is right only for unsigned and for non-negative numbers, e.g. +5 = 0101 → 0000 0101.

signal-flow.title: Values propagate through a NAND circuit level by level
signal-flow.intro: A two-level NAND circuit, G1 = NAND(A, B), G2 = NAND(A, C), F = NAND(G1, G2).

elements.text: Signals flow one gate delay at a time

steps.caption: t = 0: the inputs change to A = 1, B = 0, C = 1. The gate outputs still show their old values for one gate delay.
t = 1 gate delay: the first level settles. G1 = (A·B)′ = 1, G2 = (A·C)′ = 0.
t = 2 gate delays: the output gate sees settled inputs. F = (G1·G2)′ = (1·0)′ = 1. The circuit is AB + AC, and A(B + C) = 1·1 = 1 agrees.
The longest input-to-output path passes through two gates, so the output is valid two gate delays after the inputs change: that is the circuit's propagation delay.

staircase-switch.title: A staircase (two-way switch) circuit computes XNOR
staircase-switch.intro: Each two-way switch connects its pivot to the top terminal b (ON, 1) or the bottom terminal c (OFF, 0). The b terminals are wired together, and so are the c terminals.

elements.text: Two staircase switches: the lamp is XNOR

steps.caption: S1 = 1, S2 = 1: both blades touch the same wire, the loop closes, the lamp is on.
S1 = 1, S2 = 0: the blades touch different wires, the loop is open, the lamp is off. Flipping either switch now toggles the lamp.
S1 = 0, S2 = 0: both blades touch the same wire, the loop closes, the lamp is on.
S1 = 0, S2 = 1: the blades touch different wires, the loop is open, the lamp is off.
The lamp is on exactly when the two switches agree: L = S1 ⊙ S2 = S1·S2 + S1′·S2′. Swapping the wires (b to c) gives XOR instead; either way each switch toggles the lamp.

switch-model.title: Switches and a lamp: series is AND, parallel is OR
switch-model.intro: Two switches, A and B, wired in series (left) and in parallel (right). A closed switch is 1, an open one is 0; a lit lamp is 1.

elements.text: Switches and a lamp: series is AND, parallel is OR

steps.caption: A = 0 (open), B = 0 (open). Series: the lamp is off, an open switch breaks the only path. Parallel: the lamp is off, both paths are open.
A = 0 (open), B = 1 (closed). Series: the lamp is off, an open switch breaks the only path. Parallel: the lamp is on, at least one path is closed.
A = 1 (closed), B = 0 (open). Series: the lamp is off, an open switch breaks the only path. Parallel: the lamp is on, at least one path is closed.
A = 1 (closed), B = 1 (closed). Series: the lamp is on, both switches are closed. Parallel: the lamp is on, at least one path is closed.
The finished table: the series lamp is the AND of the switches (on only when both are closed); the parallel lamp is the OR (on when at least one is closed).

twos-complement-wheel.title: The 2's-complement wheel
twos-complement-wheel.intro: Sixteen 4-bit patterns arranged clockwise in counting order, 0000 at the top. The number inside the ring next to each pattern is its unsigned value, 0 to 15.

steps.caption: Each clockwise step adds 1. From 0000 to 0111 the patterns count 0 to 7, exactly as unsigned numbers.
Now step backwards from 0000: one step anticlockwise lands on 1111. A step back means −1, so it is natural to read 1111 as −1, not 15.
Reading every pattern with a leading 1 as (unsigned value − 16) gives 2's complement: 1111 = −1, 1110 = −2, …, 1000 = −8. The top bit now says the sign.
The only jump is the seam at the bottom: 0111 (+7) is followed by 1000 (−8). Crossing it is overflow. 4-bit 2's complement covers −8 … +7, sixteen different values, one zero.
Sign-magnitude reads the top bit as a sign and the other three as a size: 1000 is −0 and 1111 is −7. Two patterns mean zero, so only 15 values fit (−7 … +7).
1's complement negates by flipping every bit: 1111 is −0 and 1000 is −7. Again two zeros and the range −7 … +7.
Back to 2's complement: one zero, no gaps, and the wheel's clockwise steps are ordinary addition. That is why every modern machine uses it.

ulp-precision.title: The gap between neighbours doubles every binade
ulp-precision.intro: Positive values of a toy floating-point format with a hidden bit and 2 fraction bits, from 1/2 up to 8, marked on a number line.

elements.text: A toy float with 2 fraction bits: 4 values in every binade

elements.label: relative gap: gap ÷ start of binade

steps.caption: Binade [1, 2): the exponent is fixed and the 2 fraction bits give 4 values, 1, 5/4, 3/2, 7/4. Neighbours are 1/4 apart: one ulp = 2^(E − 2) with E = 0.
Binade [2, 4): the exponent is fixed and the 2 fraction bits give 4 values, 2, 5/2, 3, 7/2. Neighbours are 1/2 apart: one ulp = 2^(E − 2) with E = 1.
Binade [4, 8): the exponent is fixed and the 2 fraction bits give 4 values, 4, 5, 6, 7. Neighbours are 1 apart: one ulp = 2^(E − 2) with E = 2.
Binade [1/2, 1): the exponent is fixed and the 2 fraction bits give 4 values, 1/2, 5/8, 3/4, 7/8. Neighbours are 1/8 apart: one ulp = 2^(E − 2) with E = -1.
Every binade holds the same 4 values, so each step up doubles the gap: 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1. The largest gap is in the top binade.
Divide each gap by the start of its binade: (1/8)/(1/2) = (1/4)/1 = (1/2)/2 = 1/4 = 2⁻². The relative gap is the same everywhere: that is floating point's promise.

vem-unfold.title: Unfolding a variable-entered map into a K-map
vem-unfold.intro: A 2 × 2 variable-entered map for f(A, B, C): rows A, columns B, entered variable C. Entries: C, 1 (top row); 0, C′ (bottom row).

elements.text: A variable-entered map and its unfolded K-map

steps.caption: A variable-entered map for f(A, B, C) uses only A and B as map variables. Each cell holds what f is as a function of the entered variable C for that A, B: 0, 1, C or C′.

set.text: cell = f(A, B, C) as a function of C

steps.caption: Unfold it: each VEM cell becomes two cells of the full map, C = 0 and C = 1. Cell A = 0, B = 0 holds C, so f(0, 0, 0) = 0 and f(0, 0, 1) = 1; cell A = 0, B = 1 holds 1, so both are 1; cell A = 1, B = 0 holds 0; cell A = 1, B = 1 holds C′, so only C = 0 gives 1.
Group the full map: m1, m3 (A = 0, C = 1) give A′C; m2, m6 (B = 1, C = 0) give BC′.

Read directly from the VEM: the 1 at A = 0, B = 1 is a don't-care for the C-group and for the C′-group. C at (0, 0) with that 1 gives A′·C; C′ at (1, 1) with that 1 gives B·C′. Same answer, without unfolding.

set.text: C-loop: A′ → A′C;  C′-loop: B → BC′

xnor-chain.title: XNOR chains and XOR chains agree for an odd number of variables
xnor-chain.intro: Truth table of x ⊕ y ⊕ z, the chain x ⊙ y ⊙ z, and a 3-input XNOR gate (the complement of the 3-input XOR).

elements.text: Chains of XNOR vs XOR, three variables
With three variables the XNOR chain equals the XOR chain; a 3-input XNOR gate (XNOR₃) is their complement.
Odd n: chain ⊙ = chain ⊕. XNOR₃ gate = complement.

xor-controlled-inverter.title: XOR as a controlled inverter
xor-controlled-inverter.intro: An XOR gate with a data input x and a control input c.

steps.caption: c = 0, x = 0: the output is 0 ⊕ 0 = 0. With the control at 0 the gate passes x unchanged.
c = 0, x = 1: the output is 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. With the control at 0 the gate passes x unchanged.
c = 1, x = 0: the output is 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. With the control at 1 the gate inverts x.
c = 1, x = 1: the output is 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. With the control at 1 the gate inverts x.
So x ⊕ 0 = x and x ⊕ 1 = x′. This is why XOR complements a bit on demand: in adder-subtractors, in parity generators and in the 'flip if differ' tricks of this lesson.

xor-delay-timing.title: Timing diagram of two XOR edge-detector stages
xor-delay-timing.intro: A circuit of two stages: P = A ⊕ A delayed by 1, then B = P ⊕ P delayed by 3. XOR gates and wires have no delay.

elements.text: Edge detectors: XOR with a delayed copy

steps.caption: Input A: 0 until t = 1, then 1 for ever. (Everything is 0 before t = 0.)
A buffer delays A by 1: its output rises at t = 2.
P = A ⊕ (delayed A) is 1 only while the two differ: from t = 1 to t = 2. A single edge of A becomes a pulse whose width is the delay.
A second buffer delays P by 3: a copy of the pulse from t = 4 to t = 5.
B = P ⊕ (delayed P) is 1 wherever exactly one pulse is high: [1, 2) and [4, 5). B changes level 4 times between t = 0 and t = 8.

set.text: B: 0→1 at 1, 1→0 at 2, 0→1 at 4, 1→0 at 5: 4 transitions

xor-from-nand.title: XOR built from four NAND gates
xor-from-nand.intro: Four 2-input NAND gates: G1 is shared by G2 and G3, and G4 combines them.

steps.caption: Algebra: G2 = (A·(AB)′)′ = A′ + AB = A′ + B and G3 = A + B′, so F = ((A′ + B)(A + B′))′ = (AB + A′B′)′ = A ⊕ B. An exhaustive search confirms that no circuit of three 2-input NANDs computes XOR.

set.text: F = A ⊕ B with 4 NANDs (the minimum)

xor-parity-chain.title: A chain of XOR gates computes the parity of its inputs
xor-parity-chain.intro: Four inputs A, B, C, D = 1, 0, 1, 1 enter a chain of three 2-input XOR gates.

elements.text: A chain of XORs computes parity

steps.caption: Gate 1: 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. The running value is the parity of the inputs so far (1, 0: 1 one, odd).
Gate 2: 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. The running value is the parity of the inputs so far (1, 0, 1: 2 ones, even).
Gate 3: 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. The running value is the parity of the inputs so far (1, 0, 1, 1: 3 ones, odd).
The final output is 1 because three of the four inputs are 1, an odd number. An XOR of any number of inputs is 1 exactly when an odd number of them are 1.
